subject: biology
title: Specialised Cells
welcome_lead: Meet sperm, eggs, red blood cells, neurones and more — each built for a special job.
meta_desc: KS3 Biology adventure on specialised cells and their adaptations.
final_note: You can now describe several specialised cells and how their shape fits their job.

walkthroughs.body_html: Sperm cells have a tail and many mitochondria for swimming. Red blood cells are disc-shaped with no nucleus to carry more oxygen. Neurones are long to carry signals.
Root hair cells have a long extension to absorb more water. Palisade cells in leaves are full of chloroplasts for fast photosynthesis.
Each cell's shape matches its role. A neurone is long because messages travel far. A red blood cell is small and flat to slip through tiny vessels.

mcqs.q: Can sucrose move in both directions in the phloem?
options: Phloem always carries sucrose downwards from leaves to roots.
Phloem carries water upwards and sucrose downwards in the same tube.
Yes — translocation goes from any source (e.g. leaves) to any sink (e.g. roots, fruits), so direction varies seasonally and between phloem sieve tubes.

mcqs.q: Where do plants get most of their biomass from?
options: Plants gain most of their mass directly from sunlight, which has weight.
The body produces a different, more powerful antibody during the secondary response.
Plants get most of their mass from the soil through their roots.
From carbon dioxide in the air — the carbon in plant tissue comes mostly from CO2 fixed during photosynthesis.

mcqs.q: Why is the secondary immune response to a pathogen faster and stronger than the primary?
options: The pathogen becomes weaker after the primary exposure, so the body has an easier job.
Memory cells generated during the primary response can rapidly proliferate and produce large amounts of specific antibody on re-exposure.
The body produces a different, more powerful antibody during the secondary response.
Phloem carries water upwards and sucrose downwards in the same tube.
